rome.overview:
Polity: the Roman Republic (res publica).

Date of record: 278 BCE (middle of the Pyrrhic War; Romans defeated at Asculum 279, refused peace, campaigned on).

Scope at the date: peninsular Italy south of the Po, an alliance system of Latin and Italian socii; no overseas provinces yet (provincia = a sphere of duty, not a territory).

Evidence base: primary literary (Polybius, Livy, Plutarch, Cicero, Diodorus); the consular Fasti; modern scholarship. Date-drift warning: Polybius' account of the Roman "mixed constitution" describes the mid-2nd century BCE, and Livy's later books describe later arrangements; both must be back-dated with care.

carthage.overview:
Polity: Carthage (Qart-ḥadašt), a commercial city-state with a maritime empire (North Africa, western Sicily, Sardinia, Iberian coasts).

Date of record: 278 BCE — during the war with Syracuse/Pyrrhus. Carthage besieged Syracuse by land and sea in 278 and withdrew when Pyrrhus landed (Diodorus 22). The same years saw a Carthago-Roman accord (279/278) to aid each other against Pyrrhus and not to make separate peace.

Scope at the date: the city and its epikrateia; directly ruled Libyans, subject cities, and allies (socii); a navy larger than Rome's.

Evidence base: primary literary (Aristotle, Politics II.11 — c. 330 BCE date-drift; Polybius 6.51–56 — mid-2nd-century date-drift; Diodorus; Justin); very few contemporary Punic documents. Every claim about the Carthaginian constitution at 278 is at best Reconstructed from a 4th- or 2nd-century description.

epirus.overview:
Polity: the Epirote League (koinon ton Epeiroton) — a federal league of Epirote tribes (chiefly Molossians, Thesprotians, Chaonians) — under the kingship of the Molossian Aiakid house, whose king Pyrrhus was its hegemon.

Date of record: 278 BCE — Pyrrhus is in Sicily (crossed 278, invited by Syracuse against Carthage), where he was made commander/king against the Carthaginians; his son Ptolemy governed in Epirus as regent. This is the hinge between the Italian campaign (280–275) and the Sicilian venture (278–276).

Scope at the date: Epirus (NW Greece), with influence over southern Illyria, Acarnania, and (intermittently) Thessaly/Macedon; the king's expeditionary armies operate abroad (Italy, Sicily).

Evidence base: literary (Plutarch Pyrrhus, Diodorus, Justin, Polybius); epigraphic (the federal and tribal decrees of the Epirote/Molossian state — the key documents for the magistracies); coins. Date-drift warning: many federal-institution inscriptions are 3rd–2nd century; the 278 form is reconstructed from them plus the narrative.

macedonian-claimants.overview:
Polity: Macedon (the Macedonian kingdom).

Date of record: 278 BCE — a kingship in contest. Ptolemy Keraunos, king 281–279, was killed fighting the Gauls (279); Meleager and Antipater Etesias followed briefly; Sosthenes held effective power as commander (279–277) without taking the crown; Antigonus II Gonatas — son of Demetrius Poliorcetes, grandson of Antigonus I — was not yet securely king (he takes firm power and the title about 277/276, after defeating the Gauls at Lysimachia in 277). The Gallic invasion is the dominant fact.

Scope at the date: the Macedonian homeland (with its cities), with claims over Thessaly, the Thracian coast, and Greece; the "fetters of Greece" (Corinth, Chalcis, Demetrias) are the strategic prizes of the Antigonid position. In 278 the homeland is fragmented and raided, not the stable Kingdom of the later Antigonids.

Evidence base: literary (Diodorus, Justin, Plutarch Demetrius/Pyrrhus, Polybius on the Antigonid settlement); inscriptions (civic decrees, the "diagramma" of Philip V is later); coins. Date-drift warning: much detail on Antigonid institutions (the diagramma, the royal administration) is Hellenistic-late; the 278 court is reconstructed from earlier practice.

seleucids.overview:
Polity: the Seleucid Empire (the basileia of the Seleucids).

Date of record: 278 BCE — Antiochus I Soter (co-regent from ~292/291; sole basileus from 281 after Seleucus I Nicator's assassination). The Gallic invasion of Anatolia (278/277) is in progress; his victory over the Galatians (the "Elephant Battle") is still in the future (~275/274).

Scope at the date: from the Aegean coast of Anatolia to the Iranian plateau and Bactria/Sogdiana — the largest of the Successor states; the upper satrapies (Media, Persis, Parthia, Bactria, Aria, Arachosia, Drangiana, Carmania, Hyrcania) and the western centres (Antioch, Seleucia- on-the-Tigris). Control of western Anatolia is contested with Ptolemaic Egypt and local dynasts.

Evidence base: literary (Appian Syr., Diodorus, Justin, Polybius, Strabo, Plutarch), Babylonian cuneiform (the Astronomical Diaries, Seleucid-era chronicles), Greek inscriptions (civic decrees, royal letters), coins (royal portrait types, mints). Date-drift warning: most detail on Seleucid administration is 2nd-century-BCE (Polybius, and the later "seleucid administrative" picture); the 3rd-century court is more thinly attested.

ptolemaic-egypt.overview:
Polity: the Ptolemaic Kingdom (Egypt under the Macedonian dynasty of the Ptolemies) — a Hellenistic monarchy.

Date of record: 278 BCE, under Ptolemy II Philadelphus (co-regent 284, sole ruler 282). The first Ptolemaia festival (quadrennial, in honour of the deified Ptolemy I) falls at 279/278. Greek and Egyptian legal practice begin to be formally "received" around this period.

Scope at the date: Egypt, Cyprus, Cyrenaica (influence), and Aegean possessions; a top-tier navy; rivalry with the Seleukids (the First Syrian War is a few years off).

Evidence base: contemporary papyri (the Zenon archive, 260s–250s — date-drift), inscriptions, coins; court poetry (Theocritus, Callimachus); later literary sources. Most administrative detail is reconstructed from the mid-3rd century and later, so claims about 278 carry a date-drift flag.

syracuse.overview:
Polity: Syracuse (Greek polis), the leading Greek city of Sicily.

Date of record: 278 BCE — Syracuse is besieged by Carthage, and the Syracusans (led by Thoenon and Sostratus) invite Pyrrhus to take command; he crosses from Italy in 278, is made commander/king (strategos autokrator / basileus in effect), and drives the Carthaginians back. The Mamertines (Campanian mercenaries) hold Messana. Hiero II is not yet in power (he rises after 275).

Scope at the date: Syracuse and a Sicilian domain over other Greek cities (and, historically, subject/garrisoned towns), contested with Carthage in the west and the Mamertines in the north-east.

Evidence base: literary (Diodorus, Plutarch Pyrrhus, Justin, Polybius, later Cicero Verrines on the province — date-drift); coins; sparse inscriptions. Date-drift warning: much Syracusan constitutional detail comes from earlier (5th–4th c.) and later (Roman-period) sources; the 278 form is reconstructed.

aetolian-league.overview:
Polity: the Aetolian League (koinon tōn Aitōlōn), a confederation (federal league) of Aetolian tribes and later of affiliated communities/cities.

Date of record: 278 BCE. Chronological note: the Gallic invasion culminated at Delphi in late 279 BCE; the Aetolians played a major role in harrying the retreating Gauls (the “Kokkalia” phase) and the league consolidated its position in central Greece by 278. Pyrrhus was in Sicily in 278. No abrupt constitutional reform is attested at 278; institutions are the 4th–early 3rd century federal structure.

Evidence base: literary (Polybius, Livy, Diodorus, Justin, Pausanias) — much later than 278; inscriptions (federal/decree epigraphy, 3rd–2nd century BC) provide the institutional form but many details postdate 278. Date-drift warning: reconstructive in places; many “classical” descriptions reflect the mid-late 3rd century.

maurya.overview:
Polity: the Maurya Empire (Mauryavamsa), founded by Chandragupta Maurya; at 278 BCE it is under the reign of Bindusara (Amitraghāta).

Date of record: 278 BCE. Chronology (conventional, with margin of error ±1–2 years): Chandragupta’s accession c. 322 BCE; Bindusara acc. c. 297 BCE; Ashoka acc. c. 273 BCE (with 4-year interval to consecration c. 269/268). Therefore 278 BCE = late reign of Bindusara (c. 19 years into his reign). Do not project Ashokan edicts/institutions (post-261 context, esp. Dhamma-mahāmātras) backward into 278 BCE.

Evidence base: indigenous textual (Arthashastra — composite text with layers; Purāṇas; Buddhist Dīpavaṃsa/Mahāvaṃsa later; Aśokāvadāna later), foreign (Megasthenes’ Indica fragments c. 302 BCE under Chandragupta; Deimachos under Bindusara — very fragmentary), epigraphy (Ashokan edicts post-257 BCE; no extant Bindusara inscriptions). Date-drift warning: Arthashastra ideal-type; later traditions often retroject Ashokan practices. Treat as Reconstructed/Uncertain where pre-Ashokan attestation lacking.
